text:
I reject the motion. If an assistant's choices make people's lives go better, handing them over costs nothing that matters morally. What makes a life go well is the happiness and satisfaction in it. If an assistant chooses meals that keep you healthier and replies that keep friendships warmer, your life is going better by the measure that counts, and the source of the choice adds nothing to the total.

Mill valued individuality, but he valued it because it tends to make people happier and societies more inventive. Where delegation leaves people with more time and energy for what they care about, it serves the same ends individuality was meant to serve. A person with severe anxiety for whom each small choice is distressing gains a calmer life from delegation, and nothing in that is a loss.

A Virtue Ethicist will object that practical wisdom exists only in the person who exercises it, so a life of delegated choices is one in which you never become anyone in particular. If people became less capable and that left them worse off, the utilitarian would count it. But that is an empirical risk to be watched, and many people delegate small choices precisely so they can put their judgement into larger ones. Everything else is a means. What matters is the suffering prevented and the happiness made possible.

The motion overstates the cost. Where an assistant chooses better, people are better off, and being better off is what matters. Mill valued individuality, but he valued it because it tends to make people happier and societies more inventive. Where delegation leaves people with more time and energy for what they care about, it serves the same ends individuality was meant to serve.

If delegation did weaken people's ability to choose in ways that later made them worse off, that would be a real cost, and it should be measured. But that is a claim about consequences, to be tested, not a cost that exists however well things go. A carer who lets an assistant handle shopping and bills has an extra hour each day with the person she looks after.

A Stoic will object that the faculty that judges impressions is the only thing truly yours, and no better outcome can repay handing it over. That treats one faculty as valuable in itself, whatever difference it makes to anyone. If exercising it made people no happier and no better off, it would be hard to say what its value consisted in. Count everyone affected, give each the same weight, and the right policy is the one with the better total.

A utilitarian should oppose this motion. Better choices mean more welfare, and the satisfaction of having chosen yourself is only one preference to weigh among many. Some people do enjoy deciding, and that enjoyment counts. But many find daily choices draining, and for them delegation removes a burden. A blanket claim that delegation always costs something ignores the people for whom choosing was the cost.
